statement: Cones and cylinders which are of the same height are to one another as their bases.
heath_proof: Let there be cones and cylinders of the same height, let the circles ABCD, EFGH be their bases, KL, MN their axes and AC, EG the diameters of their bases; I say that, as the circle ABCD is to the circle EFGH, so is the cone AL to the cone EN. For, if not, then, as the circle ABCD is to the circle EFGH, so will the cone AL be either to some solid less than the cone EN or to a greater. First, let it be in that ratio to a less solid O, and let the solid X be equal to that by which the solid O is less than the cone EN; therefore the cone EN is equal to the solids O, X. Let the square EFGH be inscribed in the circle EFGH; therefore the square is greater than the half of the circle. Let there be set up from the square EFGH a pyramid of equal height with the cone; therefore the pyramid so set up is greater than the half of the cone, inasmuch as, if we circumscribe a square about the circle, and set up from it a pyramid of equal height with the cone, the inscribed pyramid is half of the circumscribed pyramid, for they are to one another as their bases, [XII. 6] while the cone is less than the circumscribed pyramid. Let the circumferences EF, FG, GH, HE be bisected at the points P, Q, R, S, and let HP, PE, EQ, QF, FR, RG, GS, SH be joined. Therefore each of the triangles HPE, EQF, FRG, GSH is greater than the half of that segment of the circle which is about it. On each of the triangles HPE, EQF, FRG, GSH let there be set up a pyramid of equal height with the cone; therefore, also, each of the pyramids so set up is greater than the half of that segment of the cone which is about it. Thus, bisecting the circumferences which are left, joining straight lines, setting up on each of the triangles pyramids of equal height with the cone, and doing this continually, we shall leave some segments of the cone which will be less than the solid X. [X. 1] Let such be left, and let them be the segments on HP, PE, EQ, QF, FR, RG, GS, SH; therefore the remainder, the pyramid of which the polygon HPEQFRGS is the base and the height the same with that of the cone, is greater than the solid O. Let there also be inscribed in the circle ABCD the polygon DTAUBVCW similar and similarly situated to the polygon HPEQFRGS, and on it let a pyramid be set up of equal height with the cone AL. Since then, as the square on AC is to the square on EG, so is the polygon DTAUBVCW to the polygon HPEQFRGS, [XII. 1] while, as the square on AC is to the square on EG, so is the circle ABCD to the circle EFGH, [XII. 2] therefore also, as the circle ABCD is to the circle EFGH, so is the polygon DTAUBVCW to the polygon HPEQFRGS. But, as the circle ABCD is to the circle EFGH, so is the cone AL to the solid O, and, as the polygon DTAUBVCW is to the polygon HPEQFRGS, so is the pyramid of which the polygon DTAUBVCW is the base and the point L the vertex to the pyramid of which the polygon HPEQFRGS is the base and the point N the vertex. [XII. 6] Therefore also, as the cone AL is to the solid O, so is the pyramid of which the polygon DTAUBVCW is the base and the point L the vertex to the pyramid of which the polygon HPEQFRGS is the base and the point N the vertex; [V. 11] therefore, alternately, as the cone AL is to the pyramid in it, so is the solid O to the pyramid in the cone EN. [V. 16] But the cone AL is greater than the pyramid in it; therefore the solid O is also greater than the pyramid in the cone EN. But it is also less: which is absurd. Therefore the cone AL is not to any solid less than the cone EN as the circle ABCD is to the circle EFGH. Similarly we can prove that neither is the cone EN to any solid less than the cone AL as the circle EFGH is to the circle ABCD. I say next that neither is the cone AL to any solid greater than the cone EN as the circle ABCD is to the circle EFGH. For, if possible, let it be in that ratio to a greater solid O; therefore, inversely, as the circle EFGH is to the circle ABCD, so is the solid O to the cone AL. But, as the solid O is to the cone AL, so is the cone EN to some solid less than the cone AL; therefore also, as the circle EFGH is to the circle ABCD, so is the cone EN to some solid less than the cone AL: which was proved impossible. Therefore the cone AL is not to any solid greater than the cone EN as the circle ABCD is to the circle EFGH. But it was proved that neither is it in this ratio to a less solid; therefore, as the circle ABCD is to the circle EFGH, so is the cone AL to the cone EN. But, as the cone is to the cone, so is the cylinder to the cylinder, for each is triple of each; [XII. 10] Therefore also, as the circle ABCD is to the circle EFGH, so are the cylinders on them which are of equal height.
ai_proof_text:
12.11
**Statement:** Cones and cylinders which are of the same height are to one another as their bases.

**Step 1.** Let there be cones and cylinders of the same height, whose bases are the circles ABCD, EFGH [D11.20, D11.23]; let K, M be the centres of these circles, KL, MN the axes of the cones [D11.19], L, N their vertices, and AC, EG diameters of the bases; call the cones AL and EN, and let the cylinders be those standing on the bases ABCD, EFGH with the same height. Because the axis of a cone is the fixed side of the generating right-angled triangle and is at right angles to the side which describes the base [D11.18], the axes KL, MN are perpendicular to the planes of the bases and are the heights of the cones [D6.4]; by hypothesis these heights are equal. I say that, as the circle ABCD is to the circle EFGH, so is the cone AL to the cone EN, and so is the cylinder on ABCD to the cylinder on EFGH.

**Step 2.** Suppose the circle ABCD is not to the circle EFGH as the cone AL is to the cone EN. Then let it be contrived that, as the circle ABCD is to the circle EFGH, so is the cone AL to some solid O, where O is not equal to the cone EN; O is therefore either less or greater than the cone EN.

**Step 3.** First let O be less than the cone EN, and let the solid X be the excess by which the cone EN exceeds O, so that the cone EN is equal to O and X together.

**Step 4.** Inscribe in the circle EFGH the square EFGH [4.6]; by that construction its diagonals EG, FH are diameters of the circle. Circumscribe about the circle a square [4.7]; each side of the circumscribed square is equal to the diameter of the circle [4.7], so the circumscribed square is equal to the square on EG. Since the angle EFG is right, the square on EG is equal to the squares on EF, FG together [1.47], and since EF is equal to FG this is double the square EFGH. Hence the square EFGH is half the circumscribed square. The circle lies within the circumscribed square, because each side of that square touches the circle without cutting it [D3.2]; so the circle is less than the circumscribed square [CN5]. Therefore the square EFGH is greater than half the circle EFGH.

**Step 5.** On the square EFGH set up a pyramid with vertex N, and on the circumscribed square set up a pyramid with vertex N. Their bases lie in the plane of the circle EFGH and they have the same vertex, so they have the same height, namely the perpendicular MN from N to that plane [D6.4]. Therefore the pyramid on EFGH is to the pyramid on the circumscribed square as the square EFGH is to the circumscribed square [12.6]; hence the pyramid on EFGH is half the pyramid on the circumscribed square. The cone EN lies within the pyramid on the circumscribed square, since its base lies within that square and it has the same vertex N; so the cone is less than that pyramid [CN5]. Therefore the pyramid with base EFGH and vertex N is greater than half the cone EN.

**Step 6.** Bisect the circumferences EF, FG, GH, HE at the points P, Q, R, S [3.30], and join EP, PF, FQ, QG, GR, RH, HS, SE [P1]. Consider the triangle EPF. By the construction of 3.30, P lies on the straight line drawn from the middle point J of EF at right angles to EF, and this straight line passes through the centre M of the circle [3.1 Por.], so that M, J, P are in one straight line. Draw through P the tangent to the circle [3.17]; it is at right angles to the straight line MP joining the centre to the point of contact [3.18]. Since EF and the tangent are both at right angles to the same straight line MJP, the tangent is parallel to EF [1.28]. Complete the parallelogram on the base EF whose opposite side lies on the tangent [1.31]. The triangle EPF has the same base EF as this parallelogram and lies in the same parallels, so the parallelogram is double the triangle EPF [1.41]. The segment EPF of the circle lies within the parallelogram, since the tangent does not enter the circle [D3.2]; so the segment is less than the parallelogram [CN5]. Therefore the triangle EPF is greater than half the segment EPF of the circle; and in the same way the triangles FQG, GRH, HSE are greater than half of the segments of the circle on which they stand.

**Step 7.** On the triangle EPF set up a pyramid with vertex N, and on the parallelogram of Step 6 set up a pyramid with vertex N; their bases lie in the plane of the circle and they have the same vertex, so they have the same height MN. Therefore the pyramid on EPF is to the pyramid on the parallelogram as the triangle EPF is to the parallelogram [12.6], so that the pyramid on EPF is half the pyramid on the parallelogram. The segment of the cone EN which stands on the segment EPF of the circle, that is, the part of the cone cut off by the plane through N, E, F, lies within the pyramid on the parallelogram, so it is less than that pyramid [CN5]. Therefore the pyramid with base EPF and vertex N is greater than half the segment of the cone standing on EPF; and similarly for the pyramids with vertex N on the triangles FQG, GRH, HSE.

**Step 8.** Thus the cone EN and the solid X are two unequal magnitudes, of which the cone is the greater. From the cone there has been subtracted the pyramid on the square EFGH, which is greater than its half, and from the remainder, namely the four segments of the cone, the four pyramids on the triangles, which are together greater than half of that remainder. Bisecting the remaining circumferences, joining straight lines, setting up on each triangle a pyramid with vertex N, and continuing in this way, we shall at length leave some segments of the cone EN which are together less than the solid X [10.1]. Let such segments have been left, and for definiteness let them be the segments of the cone standing on EP, PF, FQ, QG, GR, RH, HS, SE; then the pyramid with the polygon EPFQGRHS as base and vertex N, together with these segments, makes up the cone EN.

**Step 9.** The cone EN is equal to O together with X, and is also equal to the pyramid with base EPFQGRHS together with the remaining segments; subtracting the segments from both, the pyramid with base EPFQGRHS is equal to O together with the excess of X over the segments [CN3], and this excess is a magnitude because the segments are less than X. Therefore the pyramid with base EPFQGRHS and vertex N is greater than the solid O [CN5].

**Step 10.** Inscribe in the circle ABCD, by the same construction, the square ABCD [4.6] and bisect its circumferences the same number of times at U, V, W, Z [3.30], so obtaining the polygon AUBVCWDZ similar to the polygon EPFQGRHS; on it set up a pyramid with vertex L. The height of this pyramid is the perpendicular KL from L to the plane of the circle ABCD [D6.4], which is equal to MN; so the pyramid with base AUBVCWDZ and vertex L and the pyramid with base EPFQGRHS and vertex N are of the same height.

**Step 11.** Since the polygons AUBVCWDZ, EPFQGRHS are similar and inscribed in the circles, the polygon AUBVCWDZ is to the polygon EPFQGRHS as the square on AC is to the square on EG [12.1]. But the circle ABCD is to the circle EFGH as the square on AC is to the square on EG [12.2]. Therefore, as the polygon AUBVCWDZ is to the polygon EPFQGRHS, so is the circle ABCD to the circle EFGH [5.11].

**Step 12.** Since the two pyramids are of the same height and have polygonal bases, the pyramid with base AUBVCWDZ and vertex L is to the pyramid with base EPFQGRHS and vertex N as the polygon AUBVCWDZ is to the polygon EPFQGRHS [12.6], that is, as the circle ABCD is to the circle EFGH [5.11]. But the circle ABCD is to the circle EFGH as the cone AL is to the solid O (Step 2). Therefore, as the cone AL is to the solid O, so is the pyramid with base AUBVCWDZ and vertex L to the pyramid with base EPFQGRHS and vertex N [5.11].

**Step 13.** In this proportion the first magnitude, the cone AL, is greater than the third, the pyramid with base AUBVCWDZ and vertex L, for that pyramid lies within the cone and is a part of it [CN5]. Therefore the second magnitude, the solid O, is greater than the fourth, the pyramid with base EPFQGRHS and vertex N [5.14]. But by Step 9 that pyramid is greater than O: which is impossible. Therefore the circle ABCD is not to the circle EFGH as the cone AL is to any solid less than the cone EN.

**Step 14.** In the same manner, interchanging the two cones in Steps 3 to 13, it is proved that the circle EFGH is not to the circle ABCD as the cone EN is to any solid less than the cone AL.

**Step 15.** Next let O be greater than the cone EN. Then, inversely, as the circle EFGH is to the circle ABCD, so is the solid O to the cone AL [5.7 Por.]. Let it be contrived that, as the solid O is to the cone AL, so is the cone EN to some solid T. In this proportion the first magnitude, O, is greater than the third, the cone EN; therefore the second, the cone AL, is greater than the fourth, T [5.14]. Also, since the circle EFGH is to the circle ABCD as O is to the cone AL, and O is to the cone AL as the cone EN is to T, the circle EFGH is to the circle ABCD as the cone EN is to T [5.11], where T is less than the cone AL: which is impossible by Step 14. Therefore O is not greater than the cone EN.

**Step 16.** Since O is neither less nor greater than the cone EN, it is equal to it. Therefore, as the circle ABCD is to the circle EFGH, so is the cone AL to the cone EN.

**Step 17.** Further, the cylinder on the base ABCD has the same base as the cone AL and equal height, so the cone AL is a third part of that cylinder, that is, the cylinder is triple the cone AL; and likewise the cylinder on the base EFGH is triple the cone EN [12.10]. Since the same multiples of magnitudes have the same ratio as the magnitudes themselves taken in corresponding order, as the cone AL is to the cone EN, so is the cylinder on ABCD to the cylinder on EFGH [5.15]. Therefore also, as the circle ABCD is to the circle EFGH, so is the cylinder on ABCD to the cylinder on EFGH [5.11].

**Step 18.** Therefore cones and cylinders which are of the same height are to one another as their bases. Q.E.D.
